items.en: Yesterday I went to the cinema.
In summer we went to the sea.
The guests came in the evening.
Yesterday I bought a new phone.
She bought fruit at the market.
I bought these shoes in Tbilisi.
They bought a lot of presents.
Yesterday I talked with Mom on the phone.
I sent my friend a message.
In the morning we talked with grandma.
What did you do on Saturday?
In the morning I went to the market.
In the evening I made dinner.
On Sunday I saw my friends.
It was a very good weekend.
Yesterday I watched a very good film.
I saw my teacher in the street.
I saw the sea for the first time.
We met each other at the market.
What did you see in Tbilisi?
As a child I had a dog.
I really wanted to go to the sea.
As a child I loved fairy tales.
We had a lot to do.
I was hungry, but there was no food.

ka-a2-was.title: Was and Were: ვიყავი, იყო
ka-a2-was.pattern: ვიყავი · იყავი · იყო · ვიყავით · იყავით · იყვნენ
ka-a2-was.explanation: The past of 'to be': მე ვიყავი (I was), შენ იყავი (you were), ის იყო (he/she/it was), ჩვენ ვიყავით (we were), თქვენ იყავით (you were), ისინი იყვნენ (they were). Unlike the present, the past has no short form: say ფილმი საინტერესო იყო ('the film was interesting').
ka-a2-was.fact: გუშინ means 'yesterday' and გუშინწინ means 'the day before yesterday', literally 'before yesterday'.

dialogue.en: I was at home. I was ill.

ka-a2-went.title: Went and Came: წავედი, მოვედი
ka-a2-went.pattern: წავედი · წავიდა · წავედით · წავიდნენ / მოვედი · მოვიდა
ka-a2-went.explanation: The past of 'go' starts with the prefix წა- ('away'): წავედი (I went), წახვედი (you went), წავიდა (he/she went), წავედით (we went), წავიდნენ (they went). 'Came' uses მო- ('towards here'): მოვედი, მოვიდა, მოვიდნენ. In the past, Georgian verbs usually get a prefix like this, which shows the action was completed.
ka-a2-went.fact: The same root gives present მიდის ('goes'), past წავიდა ('went') and future წავა ('will go'). The prefix changes the direction and the tense.

dialogue.en: I went to the cinema with friends.

ka-a2-erg.title: Who Did It: the Ergative Case (-მა / -მ)
ka-a2-erg.pattern: დედამ ვახშამი გააკეთა · ბავშვმა ვაშლი შეჭამა
ka-a2-erg.explanation: This is one of the most famous features of Georgian. In the past tense, the person who DOES something to an object takes a special ending, the ergative: -მა after consonants (ბავშვი → ბავშვმა) and -მ after vowels (დედა → დედამ). The object, meanwhile, goes into its basic form: დედამ ვახშამი გააკეთა ('Mom made dinner'). Pronouns: მე and შენ don't change, but ის becomes მან and ისინი becomes მათ. Verbs of motion like 'went' don't use the ergative: დედა წავიდა.
ka-a2-erg.fact: Ergative marking is found in Basque, Tibetan, Hindi and most languages of the Caucasus, but not in English or Russian. In Georgian it appears only in certain tenses: in the present, the ordinary pattern returns.

dialogue.en: Dad made it. It was delicious!

ka-a2-bought.title: Bought: ვიყიდე, იყიდა
ka-a2-bought.explanation: 'Buy' in the past: ვიყიდე (I bought), იყიდე (you bought), მან იყიდა (he/she bought), ვიყიდეთ (we bought), მათ იყიდეს (they bought). Remember the ergative for he/she/they and named people: დედამ პური იყიდა ('Mom bought bread').
ka-a2-bought.fact: Open-air markets in Georgia are a favourite place to buy fresh fruit, cheese, herbs and spices.

dialogue.native: ახალი ჩანთა ვიყიდე. ძალიან იაფი იყო.
dialogue.en: I bought a new bag. It was very cheap.

ka-a2-call.title: On the Phone: ვილაპარაკე, დავრეკე
ka-a2-call.explanation: 'I talked / spoke' is ვილაპარაკე (he/she: ილაპარაკა, we: ვილაპარაკეთ). Add -თან for the person and -ით for the means: დედასთან ტელეფონით ვილაპარაკე ('I spoke with Mom on the phone'). 'I rang / called' is დავრეკე, 'he/she called' დარეკა, and 'I'll call' is the future დავრეკავ. A message is შეტყობინება; 'I sent' is გავგზავნე.
ka-a2-call.fact: The root of დარეკა is the same as რეკავს ('it rings'), so 'to phone' is literally 'to ring'.

dialogue.en: Nino called. We talked on the phone.

ka-a2-did.title: What Did You Do? გავაკეთე
ka-a2-did.explanation: 'Do / make' in the past: გავაკეთე (I did), გააკეთე (you did), მან გააკეთა (he/she did), გავაკეთეთ (we did), მათ გააკეთეს (they did). The key question is რა გააკეთე? ('what did you do?'). Answer with a list of past verbs joined by და or მერე ('then').
ka-a2-did.fact: Georgian often skips subject pronouns, because the verb already tells you who: გავაკეთე can only mean 'I did'.

dialogue.en: What did you do on Saturday?
I went to the market, then made dinner.

ka-a2-saw.title: Saw and Met: ვნახე
ka-a2-saw.explanation: ვნახე means both 'I saw' and 'I met / visited': ფილმი ვნახე ('I watched a film'), მეგობარი ვნახე ('I met a friend'). The future is ვნახავ ('I'll see'), and 'see you!' is a friendly ნახვამდის, built on the same root ('until seeing').
ka-a2-saw.fact: ნახვამდის ('goodbye') literally means 'until seeing', from ნახვა ('seeing') + -მდე ('until').

ka-a2-had.title: Had, Wanted, Loved
ka-a2-had.explanation: The 'inverted' verbs also have past forms, and the person stays in the dative: მქონდა (I had, a thing), მყავდა (I had, a person or animal), მინდოდა (I wanted), მიყვარდა (I loved), მშიოდა (I was hungry). He/she: ჰქონდა, ჰყავდა, უნდოდა, უყვარდა. ბავშვობაში means 'in childhood'.
ka-a2-had.fact: These past forms almost all share the marker -დ-: მქონდა, მყავდა, მინდოდა, მიყვარდა.

dialogue.en: Did you have a dog as a child?
Yes, I had a big white dog.
